guide.title: What is the Eisenhower matrix?
guide.lead: A way of deciding what to work on: split every task along two axes, importance and urgency, into four boxes, and handle each box differently. The longer the list gets, the clearer the point of it becomes — it settles “what not to do” before “what to do first”.
guide.quote: “I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.”
guide.quoteCite: — a line Dwight D. Eisenhower liked to quote
guide.origin: It takes its name from an anecdote about Eisenhower, the 34th President of the United States and Supreme Commander of the Allied forces in the Second World War, and became widely known when Stephen Covey wrote about it in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People.
guide.importance: Does it move your goals and results forward? Would skipping it cost you something in the long run? The measure is yours.
guide.urgency: Does it need a response right now? Is a deadline close? The measure usually sits outside you — a deadline, somebody else's request.
guide.axesNote: The two get confused constantly, and they are completely different axes. A notification going off is urgent and rarely important, while the things that matter most — health, learning, the people around you — hardly ever become urgent on their own.

q1.body: Deadlines about to land, incidents and outages, requests that need an answer today.
q1.example: e.g. tomorrow's presentation, a server outage, paperwork due today
q1.tip: A box that is always full means you are doing nothing but firefighting. The cause is usually the box below it, left too long.

q2.body: Nobody will say a word if you skip these today, and they are the ones that produce results.
q2.example: e.g. study and exercise, design and refactoring, retrospectives, keeping in touch
q2.tip: This is the box the whole matrix exists for. Without time set aside in advance it slips forever, and you end up doing it in quadrant 1 once it has turned urgent.

q3.tag: Delegate · hand off or cut down
q3.body: It looks urgent, but mostly this is somebody else's priority arriving on your desk.
q3.example: e.g. notifications demanding an instant reply, errands somebody else could run, meetings you do not need to attend
q3.tip: With nobody to hand it to, cutting it down is the answer. Batch it into one fixed slot, or turn the notifications off so it never arrives in the first place.

q4.body: Things you do out of habit that leave nothing behind. All they do is weigh the list down.
q4.example: e.g. scrolling a feed with no purpose, checking something again for no reason
q4.tip: Deleting is a decision too. If it feels wasteful, move it to a “someday” list and get it off the matrix.

steps.dump: Brain dump — write down everything in your head first. The Brain dump list above the matrix is the place for this step. Sorting comes later; here, just write things as they occur to you. Both the Work and Life matrices share this list, so you do not have to decide which side a task belongs to yet.
steps.board: Work or Life — the Work / Life toggle at the top gives you two matrices instead of one. A task joins one of them the moment you drag it down from the brain dump into a quadrant, and leaves again when you drag it back up.
steps.importance: Importance first — ask “could I skip this?” before anything else. If it does not serve your goals, it belongs in the bottom two boxes.
steps.urgency: Then urgency — is there a deadline, does it need a response right now?
steps.place: Put it in a quadrant — when it could go either way, pick the less important one. You can move it later.
steps.reserve: Book time for quadrant 2 — claim a slot in your calendar in advance. Leave this step out and the matrix is just a list.
steps.review: Come back to it regularly — rearrange the quadrants at the end of a day or a week.

points.notTheSame: Urgent is not important. The loudest thing is not the valuable one.
points.quadOne: A crowded quadrant 1 means a neglected quadrant 2. Work done early is work that never becomes urgent.
points.tooMany: Do not pile one box high. More than five in quadrant 1 is the same as having no priorities at all. When it overflows the count turns red, and the answer is not a bigger box but a shorter list — move things down to 3 and 4, push them out to 2, or delete them outright.
points.dropping: Dropping things is the point. The reason for splitting the list four ways is to clear out 3 and 4.

app.dumpFirst: Pour everything into the Brain dump first and sort it afterwards. Your head empties far faster when you are not asking “which quadrant is this?” after every line. Once it is all written down, dragging them into quadrants one by one is steps 2 and 3.
app.notStorage: The four boxes are not storage. Keep only what you have to decide about now; leave the rest in the Brain dump, or send it out by completing or deleting it. Dozens of rows in one box is not a set of priorities, it is the same list copied somewhere else. Only quadrant 1 turns red, so the other three are yours to thin out. And the app will not stop you — blocking what you write only puts it back in your head. Deciding is a person's job.
app.boards: The Work / Life toggle at the top scopes the whole window, not just the matrix. The quadrants, the counts, the history, the trash and the export all show the side you picked, and only the Brain dump is shared. It is there so work stops being in front of you once the day is over.

tasks.add: Type in the box at the bottom of a quadrant and press Enter to add a task there. The box clears itself so you can keep going, and {{mod}} + 1–4 jumps straight to the box of the quadrant you want.
tasks.order: The number in front of a task is its place within that quadrant. Drag to reorder and the numbers follow; drag it into another quadrant and it moves there. Circumstances change and so should the quadrant — drag a task up to the Brain dump and back down from the other matrix to move it between Work and Life.
tasks.edit: Double-click a task to edit its text. Enter saves, Esc cancels.
tasks.done: The circle on the left completes a task: it leaves the list and stacks up by date in the History. Its note goes with it, so you can read back what you were thinking at the time.
tasks.trash: The × that appears when you hover over a task sends it to the Trash. Nothing is gone yet and it can be brought back, so empty out quadrant 4 without hesitating.

dump.toggle: Click Brain dump in the header to open the list, click it again to fold it away. {{mod}} + 0 opens it and puts the cursor in the box. Open or folded is remembered after you quit.
dump.paste: Paste several lines at once from a notepad or a chat and each line becomes its own task. Leading list markers like -, * or 1. and blank lines are stripped for you (up to 100 lines at a time).
dump.later: Text is all you need here. Due dates, notes and completing a task only come once it is down in a quadrant. While anything is still unsorted a hollow count chip shows, even in bar mode, so you know something is waiting.

due.set: The calendar button beside the input sets a date as you add the task; for a task that already exists, click the date chip on the right to open the calendar. Delete at the foot of the calendar clears the date and nothing else.
due.colors: The chip changes colour with the time left, so urgency is something you can see: overdue is red, today orange, within three days yellow, anything further out grey. Leave the app running for days and the colour and the count roll over at midnight on their own.

note.open: Click a task and its note opens below the matrix — one note per task. Writing down why it is in this quadrant and what comes next makes the next look much quicker. A task with a note is marked, and hovering the mark previews what it says.
note.keys: A task without a note opens straight into editing. {{mod}} + Enter saves, Esc cancels. Double-click a saved note to edit it again, and Delete removes the note only — the task stays.
note.panel: Opening a note takes the room out of the matrix — the window stays the size you left it. Drag the top edge of the card to change its height, and double-click to put it back. Click the same task again, or the ✕, to close it.
note.readonly: In the History and the Trash a note shows under its task, read-only. A long one is cut to three lines and clicking it opens the rest. Restore a task from the trash and its note comes back with it.

log.history: The History stacks completed tasks by date, newest first. Restore puts one back in the quadrant it came from and Delete sends it to the trash. Move all to the trash clears what you are looking at in one go.
log.trash: The Trash keeps deleted tasks by date. Restore puts one back where it was — into the History if it had been completed — and Delete forever removes it for good. Restore all and Empty the trash do the whole list at once, and emptying cannot be undone.
log.search: Both tabs have a search box, and it searches the whole record rather than what happens to be drawn — something you finished long ago comes straight up. A hundred are drawn at a time and the rest follow from Show more at the end of the list. Nothing is being removed.

export.run: Export in the settings (⚙), or {{mod}} + E, saves the current brain dump and four quadrants to a file. Pick PDF, HTML or Markdown at the bottom of the save dialog, and once it is written Open folder takes you straight to it. It is a good way to keep the board as it stood for a weekly review or to share it.
export.what: Only the side you are on, Work or Life, goes out. The document title and the file name say which, and the brain dump is shared so it appears in both. Flip the toggle and export again if you need the other one. Completed tasks and the trash are not included — only what is live right now.

window.bar: The Shrink to the bar button in the title bar, a double-click on the title bar, or {{mod}} + M — any of the three folds the window down to a thin bar. The Work/Life toggle and the per-quadrant counts stay on it, and clicking a count chip opens the window again. It expands from wherever you parked the bar and folds back to the same place.
window.pin: Turn on Always on top and the window stays above everything else. Position, size, mode, theme and the pin are all remembered when you quit, and if you leave it as a bar it opens as a bar next time.
window.quads: Drag the edge between quadrants to resize them. The horizontal and vertical edges are shared by all four, so growing one shrinks its neighbour, and grabbing the crossing point in the middle moves both at once. The same works on the bottom edge of the brain dump and the top edge of a note — the window stays the size you left it and the matrix gives up the difference. Double-click any edge to put it back.
window.settings: The settings (⚙) in the title bar hold language, theme, export and syncing in one place. Pressing it in bar mode expands the window first. The language follows your computer the first time the app runs; once you pick one it is remembered and takes effect on the spot, with no restart.
window.keys: That is the whole keyboard: {{mod}} + M for bar mode, {{mod}} + D for the dark theme, {{mod}} + E to export, {{mod}} + 0 for the brain dump, {{mod}} + 1–4 for a quadrant, Enter to add or save an edit, {{mod}} + Enter to save a note, Esc to cancel.

guide.sync: Sign in and the tasks on this computer match your other devices. The app works as usual with no internet, and everything you changed in the meantime goes up on its own once you are connected again.
guide.syncNote: Signing out does not delete the tasks on this computer. Neither does the server going down — your tasks are always here as well.
guide.syncGear: Signing in and the sync status are behind the gear (⚙) in the title bar. Reading about it and setting it up are deliberately in different places.
guide.syncSignIn: Sign in with Google from Sync across devices in the settings (⚙). The sign-in page opens in your usual browser, not inside the app. After that there is nothing to keep track of — what you change goes up a few seconds later, and what you changed elsewhere comes down on its own.
guide.syncDot: A dot on the gear means something has not gone up yet, and it shows in bar mode too. An orange dot means there are changes only this computer has; a red dot means the server could not be reached. Either way the changes are safely stored. Open the settings to see exactly how many are waiting.
guide.syncConflict: Edit the same task on two devices at almost the same moment and the later edit is the one that stays. If that overwrites something of yours that had not gone up yet, the app tells you it did — nothing disappears quietly.
guide.syncMerge: Sign in for the first time with tasks already here and the app asks whether to merge them into the account. Say no and they are moved aside rather than deleted — the point is that signing in briefly on someone else's computer should not push their tasks into your account.
guide.syncLeave: To remove the account itself, use Delete account in the settings. The copy on the server and syncing with your other devices go away, and it cannot be undone. The tasks on this computer stay, so you can carry on without an account. Pressing it does not delete anything straight away — it shows you what will happen and asks once more.

update.auto: There is nothing to do. While the app is running it checks for a new version and downloads it in the background, and what it has downloaded is applied when you close the app. The version you are on is at the bottom of this page and beside the app name in the title bar.
update.now: If you would rather not wait, the Update ready button in the title bar restarts and applies it there and then. The button only appears once a version has been downloaded — if it is not there you are either up to date or still downloading.

matrix.crowded: A quadrant this full is the same as having no priorities at all. Block out time in quadrant 2 first.
